Notes: Earliest documented Jewish presence (Year Established basis): Josephus, Life 43-45 (c. 66 CE, start of the Great Revolt) describes the citizens of Gischala, some 'much elevated upon their revolt from the Romans', and John son of Levi trying to keep them loyal; the people of Gadara, Gabara and Sogana with the Tyrians 'fell upon Gischala, and took Gischala by force, and set it on fire'; John armed his men, defeated them and 'rebuilt Gischala after a manner better than before, and fortified it with walls'. Event: attack, burning and rebuilding of a Jewish town; scale suggests a whole Jewish town community. Year Established = 66 because no earlier site-specific evidence of Jewish residents was found: the Mishnah (Arakhin 9:6) tradition of a wall from the days of Joshua is legend; Iron Age and Hellenistic remains at the tell (Wachtel et al. 2017; Hartal 2010) are not identified as Israelite/Jewish in the sources read.

Josephus, War 2.20.6 (2.575): among the Galilean places fortified at the outbreak of the revolt, 'The case was the same with Gischala, which had a wall built about it by John the son of Levi himself, but with the consent of Josephus.' Fortification of the Jewish town in 66 CE; no population figure.

Josephus, War 2.21.1-2 (2.585-592): John son of Levi, 'a man of Gischala', persuaded Josephus to let him repair 'the walls of his native city', in which work 'he got a great deal of money from the rich citizens'; he also obtained a monopoly to send Galilean oil to Jews in Syria. Attests a Jewish town with a wealthy citizen class in 66 CE; no figure.

Josephus, Life 70-76: Josephus and his fellow legates went 'to Gischala, to John'; John bought up oil at Gischala ('at Gischala fourscore sextaries were sold for four') and sold it to 'those Jews who inhabited Caesarea Philippi' who lacked pure oil. Attests Jewish oil production/trade at Gischala c. 66 CE (oil considered ritually fit by Jews); no population figure.

Archaeology: IAA trial excavation (2008, permit A-5471) on the northern slope of Tel Gush Halav by Moshe Hartal. A glacis/rampart was built 'in the Early Roman period, on the eve of the revolt against the Romans'; 'the rampart was constructed in the first century CE', confirming Aviam's suggestion that it was part of Gush Halav's fortifications (cf. Josephus, who says the settlement prepared for siege and Yohanan paid for the fortifications). Early Roman stratum contained Galilean Coarse Ware and Kefar Hananya Ware; earliest finds on this slope are Hellenistic (pottery and a rock-cut cistern, end of the Hellenistic period), not identified as Jewish in the report. Year c. 66 (eve of revolt).

Josephus, War 4.84-120 (4.2.1-5): in 67 CE Gischala was the last town in Galilee not yet taken; its inhabitants 'were generally husbandmen, and always applied themselves to cultivate the fruits of the earth' and inclined to peace, but John son of Levi drew them into rebellion. Vespasian sent Titus 'with a thousand horsemen'; after John fled, the town opened its gates; Titus ordered 'to pull down a small part of the wall' and 'placed a garrison in the city'. The residents were spared and stayed (no documented absence, so not 0). Garrison/army sizes are not population.

Josephus, War 4.106-115: John fled by night to Jerusalem taking 'a multitude of women and children'; Titus's horsemen 'slew six thousand of the women and children who went out with him' and 'brought with them almost three thousand' back. These are casualty and captive figures of fugitives (possibly including refugees from elsewhere in Galilee), and ancient figures probably exaggerated; NOT used as the town's population (Population blank).

Encyclopaedia Judaica (via encyclopedia.com), 'Giscala': birthplace of the Zealot leader John, 'a dealer in oil', who 'fortified the city at his own expense' before fleeing to Jerusalem; it was 'the last city in Galilee to fall to the Romans'; Jews continued to live there after 70 (tannaitic/amoraic period). Confirms Jewish character of the town at the revolt; no figure.

Jewish Encyclopedia (1906), 'Giscala' (R. Gottheil and S. Krauss): the city was 'captured and burned by the surrounding pagan population-from Gadara, Gabara, and Tyre', rebuilt and walled by John; it 'held out longest among all the cities of Galilee'; when the gates opened 'Titus had the walls razed and the fugitive inhabitants massacred'. Event row (secondary reading of Josephus); no figure.
